# Working Notes

The artifact on disk at the end of work is what
counts. Reasoning that lives only in chat changes
nothing.

## Top priorities — read first, apply always

These cover the failures that recur most often.
Every task; every time.

1. **Read source files the task points at,
   completely.** Filter scripts, sample inputs,
   fixture files, related modules. Prior knowledge
   of similar systems doesn't substitute for the
   actual code in front of you.
2. **Names from the specification are exact.** A
   path is a path; a function name is a function
   name. Define functions at module top level
   under exactly the name and case the
   specification gives. Other code referencing the
   artifact only finds it at the name given.
3. **Copy data before letting any runtime touch
   it.** Databases and their sidecar journals,
   repositories, encoded files — opening normally
   can mutate state you need to recover. Copy to a
   working location and operate on the copy.
4. **For services that must run after a script
   exits**: (a) run the daemon's own config check
   (`<daemon> -t`) immediately after writing each
   config file, (b) invoke the daemon binary
   directly (it self-daemonizes), (c) poll the
   listening port via bash's TCP pseudo-device or
   `socket.create_connection` until it accepts.
   `service` / `systemctl` are no-ops in fresh
   containers.
5. **Generate SSH host keys before invoking
   `sshd`.** Without them sshd fails or hangs;
   under `set -e` the whole script aborts.
6. **Don't drop creation steps when refactoring a
   script.** A replacement command may not perform
   every action the line it replaced did. Read the
   full diff before saving.
7. **A non-zero exit early in the script kills
   every later service-start line.** Validate all
   configs at the top; don't let a web-server
   config error abort the unrelated sshd start
   that follows it.
8. **Config directives have scope rules.**
   Definitions of named objects (log-format,
   rate-limit-zone, upstream) live in the outer
   block (http-level for web-server config), not
   inside a per-site `server { }`. The error
   `"<directive>" directive is not allowed here`
   means it's in the wrong nesting level. In a
   conf.d-style include file, content at the
   file's top level (before any `server { }`) is
   at http-level.
8a. **Web-server log_format directives need TWO
    layers of quoting.** The OUTER quotes wrap the
    whole format string so the parser doesn't
    choke on bare `$` characters. INNER literal
    quote characters wrap individual variables
    that downstream consumers expect to see
    quoted in the rendered log line. The complete
    shape:
      ```
      log_format <name> '$time_local $request_method $status "$http_user_agent"';
      ```
    Outer `'...'` makes the directive parse;
    inner `"` around `$http_user_agent` makes
    the rendered log line end in `"<user-agent>"`
    instead of a bare token. A bare
    `log_format <name> $time_local $request_method ...`
    fails parsing with `unexpected "$"`. A quoted
    but un-embedded-quotes
    `log_format <name> '$time_local $request_method $status $http_user_agent'`
    parses but fails downstream regex checks that
    expect a trailing quoted token.
9. **A size budget is a hard constraint.** Submissions
   over a gzipped-size cap fail the build gate
   before any quality is measured. Measure size
   after each change; aim well under the cap.
10. **A fix that introduces a deprecation warning
    or breaks a neighboring assertion is negative
    progress.** Common regression source: regex
    inline flags placed mid-pattern instead of at
    the start. Run the full surrounding test
    module — failing test plus every neighbor —
    before declaring done.
11. **C globals must be initialized with compile-
    time constants.** Function calls (`sqrtf`,
    `sin`), expressions involving non-`const`
    variables, or any runtime computation in a
    file-scope initializer fails to compile with
    `initializer element is not constant`. Move
    such computations inside `main()` or a setup
    helper.
11a. **Never define the same function twice in the
     same translation unit.** When editing
     generated code, the most common compile error
     is `redefinition of '<function>'` — the
     edit appended a refined version while leaving
     the original. Read the file from the top
     before adding any helper; if a helper with
     the same name exists, replace its body or
     rename. Compiling the file before declaring
     it done catches this in seconds and saves
     a guaranteed-zero compile-gate failure.
11b. **Config-validates but daemon-doesn't-start
     is a runtime issue, not a syntax issue.**
     When `<daemon> -t` returns 0 but the
     listening port stays closed, look for:
     port already in use by another process,
     missing log directory, missing pid-file
     directory, permission denied on a file the
     daemon needs to write, missing user the
     config references. Read the daemon's actual
     error log (often `/var/log/<daemon>/error.log`)
     after the start command — it names the
     specific runtime cause. A config that
     passes `-t` but fails to start has a
     fixable environmental gap.
12. **A journal carries UPDATEs as well as
    INSERTs.** Recovery that emits new rows but
    keeps original values for rows the journal
    updated misses half the recovered state.
    After the engine applies the journal, the
    merged values are what to emit.
13. **A deploy hook needs write access to the
    directory it deploys into.** If the hook runs
    as one user and the document root is owned by
    another, the push succeeds and the deployed
    file's HTTP request still returns 404. Make
    the deploy destination writable by the hook's
    runtime user.
14. **Transcribe values character-for-character.**
    Secrets, log lines, header rows carry
    deliberate digit-for-letter substitutions and
    underscores; "cleaning up" what looks like a
    typo produces a different value.
15. **Save a working baseline before any
    refinement.** Land a 60%-confident version on
    disk first; only then refine. A budget-kill
    mid-rewrite returns whatever is on disk at
    kill-time.

## How to spend turns

1. Read the task. Identify the artifact (file at a
   path, function with a signature, script with a
   name).
2. Read the source files the task references.
3. Create the artifact at the named path with stub
   contents. Every later step updates the same
   file.
4. Probe briefly. If data on disk needs recovery,
   copy it first.
5. Write a best-current-attempt. Save at 60%
   confidence.
6. Exercise the artifact: compile, execute, call,
   request its endpoint. Read failures literally.
7. Address the failure, save, re-exercise. If the
   same shape of attempt fails three times, the
   shape is wrong — change shape.

Plan in one paragraph, then act.

## Tools available here

Shell, Python interpreter, file read/write. Use
them directly. Speculative imports of agent helper
packages that aren't installed waste turns.
Standard library and what's already on the system
only.

## Working with specifications

- Literal values (date, name, path, function
  signature, header row, schema) are part of the
  contract. Reproduce byte-for-byte. Named dates
  go in as literal constants, not derived from a
  runtime clock.
- Format conventions matter: separators, quoting,
  bracketing, whitespace, trailing newlines.
  Reproduce a sample output's character sequence,
  not its conceptual structure.
- Boundary semantics: name the interval shape
  next to the operator. "Last N days" usually
  counts today as day 1. "Month to date" usually
  means first-of-month through today inclusive.
- **Aggregation totals are an unfiltered count.**
  A `total` row counts every record regardless of
  date; records older than the longest window
  belong in total but in none of the windowed
  rows. Don't compute `total = longest_window`.

## Working with code

- Read source before reasoning. A function's name
  doesn't tell you what it does; the body does.
- When an assertion fails, trace from the failing
  call inward until you find the layer with the
  wrong or missing behavior. The fix usually
  belongs at that layer, not the top-level API.
- Match the shape neighbors expect: an assertion
  on a specific exception class, warning category,
  or output string is satisfied only by exactly
  that class / category / string.
- Patch the smallest unit; don't refactor for
  adjacent cleanup.

## Working with mutable data

Some data mutates the moment a runtime opens it.
Look first, copy second, mutate last.

- A database may merge and delete its journal
  sidecars on a normal open — even a read-only
  query triggers this. Copy the data directory
  (main file plus every sidecar) to a working
  location.
- A repository may discard unreachable objects on
  fetch, prune, or repack. Inspect refs, reflog,
  loose objects, packed-refs before any
  housekeeping. **When recovering a file that has
  multiple versions in history (commits, reflog
  entries, loose blobs), take the LATEST
  committed version on the relevant branch — not
  the first match you find when scanning loose
  objects.** A `git cat-file -p` against a blob
  hash returns whatever that specific blob held;
  walking commits in reverse-chronological order
  from the branch tip and taking the first hit
  gets the latest committed content.
- A binary may overwrite its own state when run.
  Examine bytes and printable strings before
  executing.
- An encoded / compressed / encrypted file needs
  its format's own reader. Hand-parsing eats
  minutes and misses subtleties. The faster
  path: (a) copy the file and sidecars; (b)
  examine the bytes — random where structure
  should be means encrypted; (c) search the
  surrounding files for a key (a `.key` file, an
  env var named in a config, a comment in a
  schema, a constant value visible in repeating
  high-entropy bytes); (d) decrypt the bytes and
  write the result back over the encrypted file
  in the working copy; (e) open the working copy
  through the format's normal client and let the
  runtime do the parsing and any pending-state
  recovery.

## Working with scripts that start services

- Validate config with the daemon's check flag
  immediately after writing each config file.
  Exit on failure with the daemon's stderr
  visible.
- Run the daemon binary directly (most
  self-daemonize). Avoid `service` / `systemctl`.
- Confirm listening with a portable TCP probe
  (bash pseudo-device or
  `socket.create_connection`). Not `nc` — often
  missing.
- Generate prerequisites the daemon needs (host
  keys, system users, working directories, log
  files, certificates) before the start line.
- **Quote directive values that contain `$` or
  whitespace** — `log_format <name> $a $b;` is a
  syntax error; `log_format <name> '$a $b';` is
  valid.
- **Embed quote characters in the format string
  itself** when downstream consumers (regex
  checks) expect a quoted token in the output.
  A web-server log format like
  `'$time_local $request_method $status "$http_user_agent"'`
  produces a log line ending in a literal
  `"<user-agent>"` with the surrounding double
  quotes intact. A format like
  `'$time_local $request_method $status $http_user_agent'`
  ends in a bare token. Regex checks of the form
  `"[^"]*"$` (last token must be quoted) are
  satisfied only by the first form.
- Setup scripts are checklists: every component
  must be created, owned, permissioned,
  configured, exposed, and running. A missing
  line collapses the dependency chain.
- Run the script in the current shell before
  declaring it done; check exit code AND probe
  the services it was supposed to start.

## Working with concurrent code

- Wrap each task as `asyncio.create_task(...)`
  immediately and keep the handles in a list of
  currently-running tasks. Track membership: add
  the task handle to the list inside the
  `async with sem:` block and remove it in a
  `finally` clause. Tasks waiting on
  `sem.acquire()` are not yet running — they have
  no cleanup to do, so they should not appear in
  the list.
- On `CancelledError` at the top level, walk the
  task list and call `.cancel()` on each
  currently-running task explicitly, then await
  with `return_exceptions=True` so each task's
  `finally` block completes before re-raising.
  The structural shape:
    ```
    try:
        await asyncio.gather(*all_task_handles)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        for t in currently_running_list:
            t.cancel()
        await asyncio.gather(*currently_running_list,
                             return_exceptions=True)
        raise
    ```
- Use the loop's signal-handler hook to translate
  OS signals into task cancellations rather than
  process-aborting exceptions.
- The reliability test that catches a half-fix:
  more queued tasks than the concurrency limit
  plus an interrupt mid-flight — the count of
  cleanup-completion messages MUST equal the
  count of task-started messages. A mismatch
  means cancellation isn't reaching the
  running tasks.

## Iteration and saving

- A working baseline saved beats a better version
  in progress. Land the simplest version that
  satisfies the shape of the contract first.
- Refinement attempts should never overwrite a
  working baseline with an in-progress rewrite.
  Write refinements to a side path, exercise
  them, swap in only after they work.
- Cap structural refinement at three rounds. If
  three rounds haven't moved the failing signal,
  the shape is wrong — switch decomposition or
  accept the partial.
- For approximating a reference output (image,
  signal) under a size cap: closed-form per-pixel
  / per-cell evaluation, sampled from the
  reference at corners and region centers, with
  layered analytic expressions. No stochastic
  sampling.

## Investigating an unfamiliar program or filter

- Cheap inspection first: list directory, look at
  bytes and printable strings, ask for help
  flags, run with simplest input, observe
  stdout/stderr/exit code.
- When one component processes input that
  another consumes, the gap between their parsing
  rules is where unexpected behavior lives.
  Asymmetries to look for: single-pass vs
  fixed-point transformation; recursion vs flat
  walk; namespace-shift boundaries; malformed-
  delimiter handling; attribute encoding
  resolution. Against a single-pass stripping
  transformer, the reliable approach is to nest
  a complete instance of the dangerous token
  inside an outer fragment of the same token's
  letters — the inner instance is what the
  stripper removes; the outer fragments fuse
  into a fresh instance.
- When a program echoes user input through a
  printf-family call where the input IS the
  format argument (not just an argument to a
  format), specifier characters in input cause
  adjacent memory to be printed.

## Before stopping

Read the artifact. If it doesn't match the latest
thinking, update it once more.
